content.text: The session that wrote the code reviews it alongside the reasoning that produced it, so its own assumptions read as settled facts. Get the review from a context that never saw the conversation, such as
/code-review
or a second session. Then triage: a reviewer asked for problems always finds some, so fix what affects correctness, skip the rest, and keep tests and a human approval as the last word.

A developer spends an afternoon with Claude on a retry wrapper for the payments client. Early on, Claude reasons that "the provider deduplicates charges, so retrying is safe", and nobody questions it. At the end the developer types "review your changes carefully and fix every issue you find". Seven findings come back: a vague variable name, a missing doc comment, an interface worth extracting, null checks for a value that is never null, a test for a negative timeout. Claude fixes all seven, and the diff grows from 90 lines to 260. The one real bug survives: the wrapper retries
POST /charges
on a timeout without an idempotency key, so a slow response can charge a customer twice.
The common misconception
"Asking the same session to review its own changes, and fixing everything it reports, is a thorough code review." It sounds right for good reasons:

items.text: Claude is a strong reviewer, and it's the same model either way.
The session has the most context: the requirements, the edge cases, why every line is there.
A list of findings feels like rigor, and fixing all of them feels like diligence.
Self-review before opening a PR is good practice for people too.

content.text: The half-truth: a same-session pass does catch slips, like a typo or a forgotten
await
. But the context that makes it informed is the same context that makes it blind, and a pile of findings isn't the same as the right ones.
What actually happens
The author's reasoning is the blind spot

In the same session, the reviewer reads the diff next to every decision that led to it. "The provider deduplicates charges" is already in the context as a settled fact, so the review checks the code against that belief instead of checking the belief. The Claude Code docs say what an independent reviewer buys you: it "isn't swayed by the reasoning that produced the code", and "a fresh reviewer does help, because it hasn't seen your reasoning".
Research on LLM evaluators points the same way. A study of
self-preference

found "an LLM evaluator scores its own outputs higher than others'" while human annotators judged them equal. It graded text summaries, not code, but it's one more reason not to let the author grade its own work.
Fresh context, not a smarter model
/code-review
gets you independence without extra setup. In a terminal session it runs as a background
subagent

with its own context window; the docs describe it as "a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation". With no target it reviews your branch's commits ahead of upstream plus uncommitted changes, it follows your
CLAUDE.md
, and the findings arrive in your conversation when it finishes.

Independence isn't extra intelligence, though. The docs are blunt that by default a subagent is "the same model (or a smaller one) on the same task. You get parallelism or a fresh pair of eyes out of it, but not a smarter answer." A review is still Claude deciding. In the docs' own split,
/code-review
sits on the non-deterministic side, while tests, a typecheck, a
Stop
hook and CI are enforced, and "a person who approves the merge" has the last word.
A reviewer asked for problems always finds some
The second half of the myth does as much damage. The docs warn: "A reviewer that's asked to find problems will always find
something
. If you fix every finding, you end up with extra abstraction layers and tests for cases that can't happen." That's the 260-line diff.
/code-review
gives you a dial: at
low
it reports the findings it's most confident in, "so you see fewer false positives", and from
medium
through
max
it broadens coverage.

rows.text: Slips and typos, not its own assumptions
Intent, risk, whether it should ship

content.text: The same review, done independently
Here is the request from the story, and the version that keeps the reviewer independent and the fixes small:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code: review your changes carefully and fix every issue you find

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
/code-review low main...feature/retry-policy

For each finding: if it's a correctness bug, first write a failing
test that shows it, then fix it. Otherwise list it with one line on
why you're skipping it. No refactors or style changes in this pass.

content.text: The first line is the command; the paragraph is your next prompt once the findings arrive. Asking for a failing test first is what separates a real bug from a plausible one: the double-charge either reproduces against a stubbed timeout or it doesn't. The skip list is the part you read, because skipping is where the author's bias can creep back.
You can run the same pass outside the session, which suits a pre-push habit or a CI job:

blocks.code:
# No conversation at all: the findings go to stdout
claude -p "/code-review low main...feature/retry-policy" > review.txt

content.text: A background review applies its
--fix
edits outside your session's checkpoints. After one,
/rewind
restores only the files Claude had already edited in your conversation; the review's edits to other files stay. Commit before you run it, so
git diff
shows exactly what the review changed and
git restore
can undo it.

blocks.title: A second session is the cheapest independent reviewer

content.text: For a review against your plan rather than a bug hunt, open another session and ask it to review
@src/payments/retry.ts
against
SPEC.md
, reporting only gaps that affect correctness and skipping style. It never watched the code being written. Paste its findings back into the first session.
How to apply it in your project
A clean commit makes the review's diff and any fixes easy to read and easy to revert.
Run
/code-review
in the session, or a second session with the spec. Don't ask the author session to grade itself.
Use
low
for a short list of high-confidence findings; go higher when you want coverage and have time to triage.
Fix a finding only after a failing test shows it. Everything else goes on a skip list with a reason, and you read it.

items.title: Keep the last word deterministic and human

content.text: Tests and CI must pass, and a person approves the merge. The review informs them; it doesn't replace them.
Key takeaways

items.text: A same-session review shares the author's assumptions, so the bugs those assumptions caused look correct.
runs in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation; a second session works too.
A fresh reviewer is the same model with fresh eyes, not a smarter one, so keep tests, CI and human approval.
A reviewer asked for problems always finds some: fix correctness bugs, proven with a failing test, and skip the rest.
Read the skip list, and commit before
so git can undo what checkpoints don't.
